claims.text: A continuous, adherent chromium-rich Cr2O3 layer forms during service on the steels of interest.
The Cr2O3 layer acts as a barrier against corrosive agents.
Formation of the Cr2O3 barrier significantly reduces the corrosion rate.
A chromium content around 10–12% may represent a threshold separating steels with and without sustained passivity.
Acidic electrolytes are representative of environments encountered in chemical-processing service.
Thermal cycling and irradiation conditions are relevant environmental factors for nuclear-power steel service.
Sufficient chromium promotes in situ formation of a dense, stable Cr2O3 layer.
The Cr2O3 film limits access of oxygen, acids, or salts to the underlying metal.
Limiting corrosive-species access to the metal slows oxidation.
Lower-chromium steels do not acquire protective Cr2O3 coverage.
Conditions that disrupt the passive film lead to higher corrosion rates.
High-chromium steels will develop a more uniform and adherent Cr2O3 passive film than low-chromium steels under identical conditions.
High-chromium steels will have lower polarization current density than low-chromium steels under identical conditions.
High-chromium steels will undergo less corrosion-associated weight loss than low-chromium steels under identical conditions.
The protective effect requires chromium above a minimum concentration capable of sustaining passive-film formation.
The protective effect may depend on pH, temperature, and irradiation level.
Other alloying elements may modify the relationship between chromium concentration, passive-film integrity, and corrosion resistance.
